title: Flo is getting into wearables | Terra
summary: Flo is getting into wearables with Google. Its own hardware could give it more control over how it collects the data used for cycle tracking.
body_markdown:
## Why not the watch or ring people already wear


In some cases, it can. Flo already[works with Oura temperature trends](https://ouraring.com/womens-health) , and the planned Google Health connection adds another route. Its own hardware needs to improve the experience enough to justify the purchase. I’d be interested in a cheaper device built around cycle tracking.


## Temperature is the reason to shape the hardware


Temperature is one measurement that gives Flo a reason to get involved in the design. Skin temperature often rises after ovulation and falls around menstruation. Repeated overnight readings can help reveal that pattern across a cycle. Alongside recorded period dates, they could give Flo more information to work with when estimating the next period. Whether a future device actually improves those estimates will need to be tested.


When we invited Flo CTO[Roman Bugaev](https://tryterra.co/authors/roman-bugaev) and[Vladislav Nedosekin](https://tryterra.co/authors/vladislav-nedosekin) to[speak at our HQ](https://tryterra.co/podcast/cto-director-of-ai-at-flo-health-roman-bugaev-vladislav-nedosekin) , Roman explained to[Kyriakos Eleftheriou](https://tryterra.co/authors/kyriakos-eleftheriou) how Flo had spent years improving its cycle-prediction algorithm, adding wearable temperature to the data it used. His team had already trained algorithms on wrist skin temperature and was also using readings from fingers.


Flo could bring that experience into the design of a device with Google. Roman pointed to watches being charged overnight, when Flo wants temperature readings. Working on the hardware together gives the companies a chance to address that problem, with Flo involved in how the measurements are collected as well as how they are used.
